outline:
This course introduces some of the foundational texts of Western literature as both a tradition to study and a category to question. We will read influential works that have inspired a lineage of later writers. Students are invited to practice critical thinking, make connections across texts and cultures, and develop the confidence to discuss complex ideas in English.

This is a rigorous and intellectually demanding course. Students are expected to give their best effort at contributing to our community as a classroom, from partner work to class discussions. Students are also expected to do all readings, participate actively, listen respectfully, and take risks in developing their own interpretations. By the end of the semester, students will be better able to analyze literary language and connect texts to broader cultural and historical questions.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

1. Explain the central stories, characters, and questions in selected course texts.

2. Develop and discuss an interpretation of a textual passage, explaining how specific words or details support their reading.

3. Compare translations or adaptations and explain how their choices change our understanding of a character, event, or idea.

scorePolicy:
Classwork portfolio & participation: 40%
Midterm exam: 30%
Final exam: 30%

The classwork portfolio is individual work completed during class, including responses to readings and classmates’ ideas. The exams assess your ability to interpret passages and support your thinking with evidence. Exam preparation guidance will be provided in advance.
materials: Students will be strongly discouraged from using generative AI as a shortcut for language production, critical thinking, and independent projects. AI should never become a substitute for your own voice or judgment. This course is a place to practice discovering ideas and making choices for yourself, which matters more than quickly generating smooth (and ultimately lifeless) English.
